title: Rama answers Parashurama
hook: Rama strings the bow, spares the sage, and one arrow spends a lifetime of merit
carry: punya: merit is real, and it runs out

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parashurama's challenge: an axe on his shoulder, Vishnu's bow in his hand, and one avatar facing the next. Your line was avatara: the divine comes down, again and again.

The king has begged and been ignored. The whole wedding party stands frozen on the road, the brides in their carriages, the soldiers with their hands near their swords. Every eye is on one young man, just married, who has been told to string a god's bow and then fight a warrior who has made kings tremble. You might expect a duel. Valmiki doesn't write one. What Rama does next is quick and quiet, and it ends with nobody hurt.
screen: `THE ROAD STANDS FROZEN.` → `A DUEL? NO.` → `QUICK, QUIET, NOBODY HURT.`

segments.voice: Rama speaks politely and firmly. But you've taken me for someone weak. Watch. He takes the bow out of the sage's hands, strings it, and fits an arrow. Then the surprise. You're a brahmin, Rama says, and related to my teacher Vishvamitra, so I won't loose this at you. But a drawn arrow can't go to waste. It will destroy one of two things: your power to move freely through the world, or the worlds of merit you've won by your austerities. You choose. And the fire goes out of Parashurama. I gave the whole earth away to the sage Kashyapa, he says, and promised not to stay on it at night. Leave me my power to move. Take the worlds I've won. Rama looses the arrow, and those worlds are gone. Here's the Hindu idea underneath. The word is punya, merit: the good that builds up from good deeds and austerity, and it can win a stay in heavenly worlds. But Hindu teaching says those worlds don't last. In the Bhagavad Gita, people who enjoy heaven come back to this world when their merit is used up. Many teachers read this scene that way: merit can be spent in a moment. And then the old warrior does what matters more. He names Rama the undying Lord, walks around him with respect, and leaves for the Mahendra mountain. The first book closes gently: Rama and Sita at home, and Bharata gone to visit his mother's family far away. It matters very soon.
screen: `RAMA STRINGS THE BOW.` · `ONE ARROW, TWO CHOICES.` · `THE WORLDS HE WON ARE GONE.` · `PUNYA: MERIT, AND IT RUNS OUT.` · `HE WALKS AROUND RAMA AND BOWS.` · then, large: `BHARATA IS FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Parashurama walked around Rama with respect, the way Hindus circle a shrine with the holy on their right. If you pray, stand and turn once slowly in place, clockwise, hands together, the way many families end their puja, and offer whatever good you did today without counting it. If you don't pray, stand and turn slowly once anyway, and let one good thing you did today go without keeping score.
Parashurama's challenge, answered. Rama strings Vishnu's bow, spares the sage, and his arrow takes only the worlds of merit the sage had won.
Your line: punya, merit is real, and it runs out. Parashurama spent his heavens and bowed to the Lord. Day five hundred thirteen, and the first book is done.

screen: `DAY 513 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DID THE PEOPLE CHOOSE RAMA?`

howItsDone: In devotional readings this episode is heard as one avatar of Vishnu meeting the next, and the Bala Kanda as the happy prelude before the Ayodhya Kanda's exile.

fork.setup: you're Parashurama. one arrow will take either your freedom to roam the earth or the heavens your austerities earned. what do you give up?
options: the heavens; merit can be spent.
fork.reveal: he gives up the worlds he'd won by austerity, then names Rama the undying Lord. Hindu texts teach that heavens won by merit end when the merit is spent.

original.note: Sanskrit puṇya: merit, the good that builds up from good deeds and austerity. it can win heavenly worlds, and it can be spent.

trapdoor: what you thought: good deeds pile up like points that last forever.
what it means: Parashurama's worlds of merit are gone with one arrow; punya is real, and it can be spent.

what a scholar hears: some scholars treat the Bala Kanda as a later layer of the epic, and see scenes like this one, where an avatar meets an avatar, as part of how Rama's divinity was drawn into the story.
